papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web page that introduces reservoir computing and the company's photonic, delay-based reservoir computer.

assertions.value: The authors state that a reservoir computer is conceptually similar to a neural network where only a small fraction is trained, and that most of the network remains fixed with only a final output layer being trained.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: A reservoir computer is conceptually similar to a neural network where only a small fraction is trained.
in the reservoir setting, most of the network remains fixed with only a final output layer being trained.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states its own definition of a reservoir computer in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that their reservoir computer uses non-linear optics and is made with a kilometer of fiber that stores optical pulses that act as the nodes in the network.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: Our version uses non-linear optics and is made with a kilometer of fiber that stores optical pulses that act as the nodes in the network.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product; the page gives no design detail, count of nodes or measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that a reservoir computer is more suitable for hardware implementation and easier to train than a traditional neural network, and that less domain expertise is generally required than for conventional networks such as convolutional neural networks.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: a reservoir computer is more suitable for hardware implementation and easier to train.
less domain expertise is generally required than building more conventional networks such as convolutional neural networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsupported comparison; the page gives no experiment or citation for it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the structure with a fixed network and a trained output layer is ideal for physically implemented networks, where making systems reconfigurable is a significant engineering challenge.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: This structure is ideal for physically implemented networks, where making systems reconfigurable is a significant engineering challenge.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although these systems could in principle be simulated with conventional computing hardware, using a physical device directly rather than a simulation has the advantage of much lower power consumption.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: While in principle any of these systems could be simulated with conventional computing hardware, using a physical device directly rather than a simulation has the advantage of much lower power consumption
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative claim; the page reports no power measurement or comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: The page gives no figure for the power consumption of its device, so the size of the advantage is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that the idea behind reservoir computing is that a complex non-linear transformation of data can produce a high dimensional solution space on which non-trivial machine learning tasks are more easily performed than on the original data, and that even random transformations can provide information much easier to process.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: performing a complex non-linear transformation on data can produce a high dimensional solution space on which non-trivial machine learning tasks can be more easily performed than on the original data.
sufficiently complex transformations, even random ones, can provide information that is much easier to process than the original data.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author-stated intuition; the page defers to a linked review for evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of the transformation, much simpler learning techniques can be used in the output layer of a reservoir than on the raw input, and that this intuition has been shown experimentally to be correct, as reservoir computing has been successful at a number of machine learning tasks, citing a linked review for examples.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, web page (single page)
quotes: much simpler learning techniques (both in terms of user expertise and computational effort) can be used in an output layer of a reservoir
This intuition has been shown to be correct experimentally, as reservoir computing has been shown to be successful at a number of machine learning tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result: the page names no task, dataset or metric and points to an external review.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer holds the review link only as the words 'this review', so the cited work is not identified in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that high connectivity is difficult to engineer in physical systems, especially two-dimensional systems like a chip, and that light addresses this because the information carried in light is constantly moving, which eliminates the need to directly connect physically distant components.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: A challenge often encountered in physical systems is the difficulty of engineering high connectivity, especially in two-dimensional systems like on a chip.
the information carried in light is constantly moving, eliminating the need to directly connect physically distant components.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the nodes of an optical neural network such as a reservoir computer are usually the packets of light themselves, so more nodes can be added by making an optical fiber longer, and that photonic networks are therefore highly scalable.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: the nodes in an optical neural network such as a reservoir computer are usually the packets of light themselves, which leads to a natural scalability.
more nodes can simply be added by making an optical fiber longer. Photonic networks are therefore highly scalable.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim of scalability; the page reports no scaling measurement and gives no limit on fiber length or noise.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not discuss loss, noise or timing limits that a longer fiber would bring.

assertions.value: The authors state that in a delay-based implementation (they refer to section 4 of a linked review) only a single nonlinear interaction is needed, independent of the size of the network.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: in a delay-based implementation (see section 4 of this review ), only a single nonlinear interaction is needed, independent of the size of the network.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement attributed to a linked review; the page gives no derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that their current approach is delay-based, owing to the relative simplicity of implementing such systems, and that as their technology matures they could develop an architecture that takes more advantage of parallel photon processing.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: Our current approach is delay-based, owing to the relative simplicity of implementing such systems
as our technology matures we could develop an architecture that is able to take more advantage of parallel photon processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the scope of its own current approach: delay-based, with a parallel architecture only as a future possibility.
assertions.reader_inference: The delay-based design is a serial design; the parallel architecture is not built, by the page's own wording.

assertions.value: The authors state that the energy of the light particles they use is high enough not to require cooling to protect them from noise caused by heat, but much lower than the energy scales of typical electronics, and that their photonic reservoir computers therefore have the potential to operate at much lower energy consumption than other approaches.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: The energy of the light particles we use is high enough not to require cooling to protect them from noise caused by heat, but much lower than the energy scales encountered in typical electronics.
our photonic reservoir computers have the potential to operate at much lower energy consumption levels than other approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of potential, not a measured result; the page gives no power figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The word 'potential' limits the claim: no measured energy use of the device is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that light interacts very little with its surroundings and can support highly non-trivial quantum superpositions, and that for these reasons optical reservoir computers could be made quantum in the sense of using quantum interference and superposition in a non-trivial way.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: Light interacts very little with its surroundings and can support highly non-trivial quantum superpositions.
systems like optical reservoir computers could be made quantum in the sense of using quantum interference and superposition in a non-trivial way.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of possibility without a design or result on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that it has been suggested that quantum systems can be advantageous to use as reservoirs, and that a small quantum reservoir can sometimes match the performance of a much larger classical reservoir.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: it has been suggested that quantum systems can be advantageous to use as reservoirs
a small quantum reservoir can sometimes match the performance of a much larger classical reservoir
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result; the text layer carries no reference and the page gives no task, size or conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The words 'can sometimes' mean the page does not claim the match holds in general.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because no quantum elements are ever trained, quantum reservoir computing naturally sidesteps the problem of barren plateaus that plague many quantum machine learning approaches.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: because no quantum elements are ever trained, quantum reservoir computing naturally sidesteps the problem of barren plateaus that plague many quantum machine learning approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no proof, citation or experiment on the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say whether the trained output layer or the readout of a quantum state can bring its own trainability limits.

assertions.value: The authors state that their current reservoir computers are completely classical devices, and that they could relatively easily be extended into the quantum domain in a way that most neural networks could not.
assertions.anchor: Photonic Reservoir Computing, web page (single page)
quotes: While our current reservoir computers are completely classical devices, they could relatively easily be extended into the quantum domain in a way that which most neural networks could not.
assertions.certainty_reason: The closing paragraph states that the current devices are completely classical, which limits every quantum statement on the page to a future possibility.
assertions.reader_inference: The extension to the quantum domain is a claim of ease, with no design or timeline on the page.

papers.title_in_file: Storing information in light - Quantum Computing Inc

assertions.value: The authors state that the information capacity of a system whose configurations appear with probabilities p_i is the information entropy, measured in bits.

(measured in bits)

assertions.value: The authors state that the most efficient way to store information is to use each of d configurations in roughly equal proportion, and that the capacity then simplifies to S=log_2(d).

papers.what_it_is: A vendor educational web page from Quantum Computing Inc explaining why light is the basis of its technology and what challenges light brings.

assertions.value: For a system that would normally transition between two states, the authors state that with N evenly spaced measurements the amplitude that builds up in each period is proportional to 1/N, so the probability of state 1 in each period is proportional to 1/N squared, and the overall probability of ever finding the system in state 1 is proportional to N/N squared, which is 1/N, and goes to zero as the number of measurements becomes large.

making the probability to measure in state 1 1 1 ( P 1 = ∣ a 1 ∣ 2 P_1=|a_1|^2 P 1 = ∣ a 1 ∣ 2 ) proportional to 1 / N 2 1/N^2 1/ N 2 .
this will be proportional to N / N 2 = 1 / N N/N^2=1/N N / N 2 = 1/ N and therefore will go to zero as the number of measurements becomes large.

papers.version_note: A company educational web page; navigation menu text precedes the article and the links and animation are not in the text layer.
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc lesson page that explains, with Hamiltonians and verbal arguments, how a Zeno blockade lets one photon block another from entering a nonlinear cavity.

assertions.value: The authors state that when G is much larger than c and a light particle i is present, the amplitude cannot build up in i, so the light particle remains outside the cavity in f, and one light particle is bounced off another.

quotes: , then we can have a Zeno blockade. The amplitude will not be able to build up in i i i so the light particle will have to remain outside the cavity in f f f .

assertions.value: The authors state that each time the Hamiltonian changes a light particle the amplitude is multiplied by a factor, that converting into p and back therefore gives the amplitude a factor of minus one, and that the amplitudes coming directly from f cancel with those coming back from p, leaving the light outside the cavity.

quotes: Therefore when the light gets converted into p p p and comes back, the amplitude has a factor of − 1 -1 − 1 .
The amplitudes coming directly from f f f cancel with those coming back from p p p , leaving the light outside of the cavity, and indeed causing the light particles to bounce off each other.
assertions.reader_inference: The page says the per-step factor is the square root of minus one and that two steps give minus one; this is the usual factor of i from the Schroedinger equation, but the page does not derive it.

assertions.value: The authors state that transferring into the cavity and back leads to a factor of minus one, and that this can be used to perform quantum logical operations known as quantum gates.
